title: How to Rotate and Care for Inline Speed Skating Wheels So They Last
thumbnail_text: Your speed wheels are wearing out too soon

scenes.heading: How to Rotate and Care for Inline Speed Wheels
scenes.sub: A ten minute routine that keeps every wheel round and fast
scenes.narration: By the end of this guide you will know how to rotate and flip your inline speed wheels so the whole set lasts far longer. You will also learn how often to do it, how to handle three wheel and Hi Lo frames, and when a wheel is really finished. Race wheels are one of the biggest running costs in speed skating. Most skaters wear theirs out long before they need to. The problem is almost never the urethane itself. It is uneven wear. The good news is that the fix is simple. Ten minutes after a session, once a week, keeps your wheels rolling round and even.

scenes.heading: How a wheel turns into a cone
scenes.narration: When you skate, you almost never load a wheel dead flat. You push to the outside. You lean into corners. And your body has a stronger side and a weaker side. Over time, this grinds the urethane into a slight cone. The inner edge wears lower than the outer edge, as you can see here. A coned wheel has less contact with the ground. It feels skittish, and it loses grip exactly when you need it most. Left alone, one or two wheels wear out while the rest of the set still has plenty of life. Then you end up throwing away good urethane.

scenes.heading: How often should you rotate?
bullets: Every one to three sessions for most skaters
Rough outdoor tarmac daily: rotate more often
A few smooth sessions a week: weekly is fine
Feel each wheel with a fingertip after skating
scenes.narration: There is no single perfect number. A good rule for most speed skaters is to rotate every one to three sessions, depending on how hard and how far you skate. If you train daily on rough outdoor tarmac, rotate more often. If you skate a few times a week on smooth surfaces, once a week is usually fine. The key is consistency. A small rotation done regularly keeps wheels even. A big rotation done rarely cannot undo damage that has already set in. After every session, run a finger across each wheel, from the inner edge to the outer edge. If you feel a clear slope, that wheel needs to move and flip. Your fingers will notice this long before your eyes do.

scenes.heading: The rotate and flip method
bullets: Lay the wheels out in order
Flip every wheel, worn edge facing out
Move the most worn wheels to easy positions
Put the least worn wheels where you push hardest
Refit, spin check, axles snug not tight
scenes.narration: On a standard four wheel frame, you do two things at once. You move each wheel to a new position, and you flip it so the worn low edge becomes the fresh high edge. First, take all the wheels off and lay them out in order on a towel, left skate then right skate. Second, flip every wheel so the worn inner edge now faces out. This alone does most of the work. Third, move the most worn wheels, usually the ones under your strongest push, to the positions that see the least wear. Fourth, move the least worn wheels into the hardest working spots. Finally, refit them and check each one spins freely. Keep your axles snug, not overtightened. An axle done up too hard squeezes the bearings and robs you of roll.

scenes.heading: Move every wheel, flip every wheel
scenes.narration: This diagram shows the idea. Each wheel moves to a new position, and each one is turned over, so it now wears its other edge. Many skaters use a front to back swap combined with a flip. The front wheel moves toward the rear, and every wheel turns over. The exact pattern matters far less than doing it consistently, and always flipping. So keep your routine simple enough that you will actually stick to it after a hard session, when you are tired and just want to go home.

scenes.heading: Three wheel and Hi Lo frames
scenes.chapter: Three wheel and Hi Lo frames
scenes.narration: Not every skater runs four equal wheels. On a three wheel frame there are only three positions per foot, so every wheel works harder and wear arrives faster. The middle wheel usually takes the most load, because it sits under your body weight for most of the stroke. A simple loop works well. Move the middle wheel to the front, the front wheel to the rear, and the rear wheel into the middle, flipping all three. Swapping wheels between your left and right skate helps too, because your two legs almost never load them the same way. A Hi Lo frame needs one extra rule. The smaller wheel cannot swap into a big wheel position without changing your pitch. So rotate the three larger wheels among themselves, and flip the small wheel in place.

scenes.heading: Keep the set matched
bullets: A set of eight covers a pair of four wheel frames
Same compound and diameter in every position
A firmer odd wheel takes extra load and cones
Rotate together, retire together
scenes.narration: Wheels are sold as a set of eight for a reason. A full set covers a pair of four wheel frames, keeps the compound identical in every position, and starts every wheel at the same diameter. That matched start is what makes rotation work. You can move any wheel to any position without changing how the frame sits under your foot. Compound matters here too. If you mix a firmer wheel into a softer set, the harder wheel will sit slightly proud as the others wear down. It takes more than its share of the load, and that is the fastest way to cone a single wheel. Keep the set together, rotate it together, and retire it together.

scenes.heading: Check the bearings while the wheels are off
bullets: Sixteen 608 bearings in a four wheel pair
Wipe grit off the shields
Spin each one and listen for grinding
A drop of light skate oil if they sound dry
scenes.narration: Every rotation is the perfect moment to look after your bearings, because the wheels are already off. A pair of four wheel skates runs sixteen 608 bearings plus spacers. They all wear at different rates, depending on position and how much grit they pick up. Wipe the grit off the shields. Spin each bearing and listen for grinding. If any sound dry, add a drop of proper skate lubricant. A light, purpose made oil keeps them spinning freely without pulling in the dust that thick greases attract. Doing the wheel rotation and a quick bearing check as one routine keeps your whole setup fast. You also catch small problems before they cost you a wheel or a bearing.

scenes.heading: Big wheels, storage and cleaning
bullets: Tall wheels show a single coned wheel as wobble
Never leave skates in a hot car or on a balcony
Wipe road grime off with a dry cloth
No harsh solvents, store cool, dry, off the ground
scenes.narration: Larger wheels, such as 110 millimetre, carry more speed, so even wear matters even more. On a set of tall wheels, one badly coned wheel throws off the feel of the whole frame. You notice it as a wobble, or a loss of confidence in fast corners. Storage matters too. Urethane does not like long spells of heat or sunlight. Do not leave your skates baking in a car boot or on a hot balcony. In an Indian summer, a set left in a parked car can be quietly ruined in an afternoon. After skating outdoors, wipe road grime off with a dry cloth, so grit stays out of your bearings. Avoid harsh solvents, which can attack the urethane. Store your skates somewhere cool and dry, off the ground.

scenes.heading: When is a wheel actually finished?
bullets: Worn down close to the hub
Coned so far that flipping gives no usable edge
Urethane gone hard and lifeless with age
Replace the whole set to keep diameters matched
scenes.narration: So when is a wheel really done? There are three signs. It has worn down close to the hub. It has coned so badly that flipping no longer gives you a usable riding edge. Or the urethane has gone hard and lifeless with age and no longer grips. Good rotation means all your wheels reach this point together. That is far cheaper than replacing them one at a time. When that day comes, replace the whole set, so your diameters stay matched across the frame. And if you ever have to mix worn and new wheels, put the newest ones in the hardest wearing positions, and keep an eye on how they even out.

scenes.heading: Rotate often, always flip, keep the set together
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: Here is the short version. Feel your wheels after every session. Rotate every one to three sessions, and always flip them when you do. Keep the set matched, and check your bearings while the wheels are off. Store your skates cool and dry. Do that, and your wheels will stay faster, last far longer, and give you a better ride every session. The full guide, with all three diagrams and the frequently asked questions, is on the LiveLica blog. You will find the link in the description.
